title: Sessions vs tokens
summary: How an app remembers who is logged in: cookies, sessions, JWTs and refresh tokens, and what logging out really does.
youWillLearn: Why a server forgets you between requests, and how a login proof fixes it
The difference between a session (the server remembers) and a token (the proof carries itself)
Which cookie settings keep that proof safe
Why logging out with tokens is tricky, and how refresh tokens make revoking possible

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.HTTP: The language browsers and servers use to talk: one request, one response, then they hang up.
glossary.stateless: Keeps no memory between requests. Each request has to carry everything the server needs.
glossary.session: A login record the server keeps (who you are, until when), found again through a session ID.
glossary.session ID: A long random string that points to a session record. Worthless to guess, valuable to steal.
glossary.cookie: A small value the browser stores for a website and sends back to it automatically with every request.
glossary.XSS: Cross-site scripting: an attacker gets their JavaScript to run on your page, with the same powers as your own code.
glossary.CSRF: Cross-site request forgery: another website makes the browser send a request to your app, cookies included, without the user meaning to.
glossary.JWT: JSON Web Token: a small piece of text plus a signature, sent as proof of who you are. Readable by anyone, forgeable by no one without the key.
glossary.signature: A stamp computed from the token's content and a secret key. Change one character of the content and the stamp no longer matches.
glossary.access token: The short-lived pass sent with each request. Usually a JWT that expires in minutes.
glossary.refresh token: A long-lived, single-purpose token used only to get new access tokens. The auth server keeps track of it, so it can be cancelled.
glossary.rotation: Each refresh token works once. Using it returns a new one, so a stolen old copy is useless and can even raise an alarm.
glossary.revoke: To cancel a token or session on the server before it would expire on its own.

steps.title: Maya opens her notes
body: Maya has just logged in to Notely, our notes app. Now she clicks My notes.
Her browser sends a request to the app server (the computer running Notely's code). The server reads her notes from the database, where Notely keeps its data, and sends them back.

callout.text: New to Notely? The 4-minute Meet Notely lesson at the start of the Data module shows the whole app, part by part.

scene.caption: The browser asks for Maya's notes. The app server fetches them from the database.

steps.title: Every request arrives as a stranger
body: Browsers and servers talk in HTTP, and HTTP is stateless: every request arrives alone, with no memory of the one before.
Maya proved who she is a minute ago. Without help, the server has already forgotten, and cannot tell her request from anyone else's on the internet.

callout.text: A busy coffee bar where the barista forgets every face the moment you step away. If you want "the usual", you have to show something each time you order.

changes: ~ App Server: cannot tell who is asking
~ Database steps back

scene.caption: A request for "my notes" arrives. The server has no idea whose.

steps.title: Log in once, carry proof after
body: The fix: check the password once, then give the browser a proof to send with every later request.
Proofs come in two families. A session: the server keeps a note, and you hold a ticket that points to it. A token: the server hands you a signed pass that carries the facts itself.

callout.text: Coat check vs festival wristband. The coat check keeps your coat and gives you a numbered ticket: a session. The festival gives you a wristband the guards only look at: a token.

changes: ~ Browser: holds a login proof
~ App Server: knows it is Maya

scene.caption: Every request now carries Maya's proof along with it.

steps.title: Sessions: the server keeps the list
body: With a session, the server makes a long random session ID, saves it in a session store next to Maya's user id, and sends the ID back in a cookie: a small value the browser keeps for one site.
The browser sends that cookie with every request. The server looks the ID up. Found: it is Maya.

callout.text: You met this in the system design course: with several servers, the session store must be shared (Redis or the database), so any server can look the ID up.

changes: + Session Store: the server's list of who is logged in
~ Browser: the proof is a session ID in a cookie

scene.caption: The cookie carries only a random ID. The real record lives on the server side.

steps.title: Cookie flags keep the proof safe
body: The server sets the cookie with a few flags. HttpOnly: page JavaScript cannot read it, so a script slipped in through an XSS bug cannot steal it. Secure: sent over encrypted HTTPS only.
SameSite=Lax: left out when another site quietly triggers a request, which blocks most CSRF tricks.

code.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: sid=8f3a9c; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=604800
code.caption: Max-Age is in seconds: 604800 is 7 days. After that the browser drops the cookie.

changes: + Bad Script: an attacker's code running on the page
~ Browser: the cookie is HttpOnly, the script cannot read it

scene.caption: Even if a bad script runs on the page, it cannot read an HttpOnly cookie.

steps.title: Tokens: a signed pass
body: The other family skips the lookup. At login, the server writes the facts into a JWT: who you are (sub) and when the pass expires (exp).
Then it adds a signature made with a key only the server side has. Anyone can read a JWT. Nobody can change it without breaking the signature.

code.caption: A JWT is header.payload.signature. This is the middle part. It is encoded, not encrypted: never put secrets in it.

changes: − Session Store and Bad Script
+ Signing Key: stamps each pass, kept on the server side
~ Browser: the proof is now a JWT

scene.caption: The pass carries the facts. The server checks the stamp instead of looking anything up.

steps.title: The catch: you can't take a pass back
body: A JWT stays valid until its exp time, wherever it ends up. If someone copies it (from a log file, a screenshot, an XSS bug), they are Maya until it expires.
And "Log out" only deletes the browser's copy. The server never kept a list, so it has nothing to cross off.

callout.text: Avoid keeping long-lived tokens in localStorage. Every script on the page can read it, so one XSS bug can leak the token of every user who visits.

changes: + Stranger: someone holding a copy of Maya's JWT
~ Browser: Maya logged out
~ Copy still works – → 30 days

scene.caption: Maya logged out, but the copied pass still works. The stamp is valid, so the server says yes.

steps.title: Short passes, plus a refresh token
body: The standard fix: make the access token short-lived, minutes rather than days. Next to it, issue a refresh token: long-lived, used only to get new access tokens, and recorded by an auth server, the service that handles logins.
Each refresh token works once and is swapped for a new one. That is rotation.
changes: + Auth Server: hands out passes, tracks refresh tokens
− Signing Key: it now lives inside the auth server
~ Copy still works 30 days → 15 min

scene.caption: Short passes for every request. A tracked refresh token gets new ones.

steps.title: Logging out, for real
body: Now logout means something. The app asks the auth server to revoke Maya's refresh token, then deletes its own copy. No new passes can be made from it, and the last access token dies within minutes.
Need someone out this second, like a fired employee? Sessions win: delete the row, and their very next request fails.
changes: ~ Auth Server: Maya's refresh token revoked
~ Stranger: the copied pass expires and is not renewed
~ Copy still works 15 min → 0 min

scene.caption: Logout revokes the refresh token. The copied pass runs out and nothing replaces it.

steps.title: Recap: what Notely uses
body: HTTP forgets, so after login the browser carries proof. A session is a record the server can delete at once. A token carries itself and cannot be taken back.
Notely uses Supabase Auth's mix: a short access token and a rotating refresh token, both kept in HttpOnly cookies, out of reach of page scripts.

callout.text: Check: where are tokens stored? Server code should identify the user with auth.getUser() or auth.getClaims(), which verify the token, never auth.getSession(). Does logout call auth.signOut()?

changes: − Stranger
~ Browser: both tokens in HttpOnly cookies
~ Auth Server: Supabase Auth plays this part for Notely

scene.caption: Short passes, a revocable refresh token, both out of reach of page scripts.

quiz.question: An app uses only long-lived JWTs: no refresh tokens, no list on the server. Someone copied Maya's token yesterday. Today Maya clicks Log out. What happens to the copy?

options.why: Logout only deleted Maya's own copy. With no list on the server, nothing marks the token as cancelled.

options.text: It keeps working until its exp time.
options.why: The server only checks the signature and the expiry. Both are still valid, so the copy still works. This is why access tokens should be short-lived.

options.text: The server sees two users with one token and blocks both.
options.why: A plain JWT setup keeps no record of who uses a token, so it cannot notice that two people share one.

quiz.question: Which cookie flag stops JavaScript on the page, including an injected script, from reading the session cookie?

options.why: Secure makes the browser send the cookie over HTTPS only. Scripts can still read it.
SameSite controls whether the cookie is sent on requests started by other sites. It helps against CSRF, not against reading.
HttpOnly hides the cookie from page JavaScript. The browser still sends it with requests, but document.cookie cannot see it.

quiz.question: A client asks: "If we fire someone, they must lose access to the admin panel immediately." Which setup makes that easiest?

options.text: Server-side sessions: delete their session rows.
options.why: The server checks the store on every request, so a deleted row means the very next request is rejected.
A 30-day JWT keeps working for up to 30 days unless you add extra machinery, like a block list checked on every request.

options.text: Tokens in localStorage, plus an email asking them to clear it.
options.why: You cannot rely on a fired employee to delete their own access. Revoking has to happen on the server.

quiz.question: Claude Code wrote server code that decides whose notes to return using supabase.auth.getSession(). What should you ask it to change?

options.text: Nothing. It is the standard way to read the user.
options.why: It is fine in the browser, but on the server it reads the session from cookies without proving the token is genuine.

options.text: Use getUser() or getClaims(), which verify the token.
options.why: Cookies come from the browser, so anyone can tamper with them. Server code must verify the token before trusting who the user is.

options.text: Move the call into the browser code instead.
options.why: Checks in the browser can be skipped by anyone. The server must decide what data each user may see.

takeaways: HTTP is stateless. After login, every request must carry proof of who you are.
A session is a record on the server, found through a random ID in a cookie. Delete the record and the user is out instantly.
A JWT carries signed facts, so no lookup is needed. But it stays valid until it expires, even after logout.
Keep access tokens short-lived and pair them with a rotating, revocable refresh token. Logout should revoke it on the server.
Store proofs where page scripts cannot read them: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies beat localStorage.
